## Statement refuted

Every finite-dimensional Euclidean quartic partition function with nonnegative coupling has a perturbation Taylor series at zero coupling with positive radius of convergence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q\sim N(0,1)$ be the one-dimensional centered Gaussian and put $U(q)=q^4/4!$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is the explicit hypothesis of the finite-dimensional Gaussian-law suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]] defines the Borel Gaussian reference law $\gamma_C$ and the partition integral $Z(\lambda)=\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[e^{-\lambda U}]$.

[F2] For a finite Gaussian covariance, polynomial insertions have all Wick-pairing moments. In one dimension with variance one, $\mathbb E[Q^{2m}]=(2m-1)!!$ and odd moments vanish. [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]]

[F3] The finite Euclidean partition integral is positive and finite for every $\lambda\ge0$, and its order-$M$ coefficients are $(-1)^k\mathbb E[U^k]/k!$. [[thm-qft-finite-asymptotic-wick-expansion]]

## Counterexample

**Given:** Use the measure and coefficients of [F1]–[F3] with $N=1$, covariance $C=1$, and $U(q)=q^4/4!$.

1.1 By [F1], $Z(0)=\int1\,d\gamma_1=1$. For $\lambda>0$, [F3] gives $0<Z(\lambda)<\infty$ and identifies the formal coefficients as $(-1)^n\mathbb E[U^n]/n!$. [A1, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 With $U(q)=q^4/4!$, [F2] gives $$a_n=\frac{\mathbb E[Q^{4n}]}{(4!)^n n!}=\frac{(4n-1)!!}{(4!)^n n!}=\frac{(4n)!}{(4!)^n n!\,2^{2n}(2n)!}.$$ The pairing count follows by pairing the first of $4n$ factors with any of the other $4n-1$ factors and repeating on the remaining factors. [F2, algebra]

2.1 Dividing successive coefficients from step 1.2 yields $$\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\frac{(4n+1)(4n+3)}{24(n+1)}\longrightarrow\infty.$$ Hence for each $\lambda>0$ the absolute term ratio $\lambda a_{n+1}/a_n$ eventually exceeds $2$, so the terms do not tend to zero and the formal series diverges at every nonzero $\lambda$; its radius of convergence is zero. [step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The exact probability measure still exists for all $\lambda\ge0$ by step 1.1, while its perturbation series has zero radius by step 2.1. This refutes the Statement without asserting Borel summability or any continuum-field result. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second-countable smooth manifold without boundary, of dimension $n$. Its cotangent bundle is

$$T^*Q=\coprod_{q\in Q}T_q^*Q,\qquad \pi:T^*Q\to Q,\quad \pi(q,p)=q,$$

with the canonical smooth structure and induced cotangent charts supplied by the manifold construction in [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]]. The **tautological one-form** is $\theta_{(q,p)}(\xi)=p(d\pi_{(q,p)}\xi)$, and the **canonical cotangent two-form** is $\omega=-d\theta$. The exact theorem [[thm-the-canonical-cotangent-two-form-is-symplectic]] makes $(T^*Q,\omega)$ a symplectic manifold in the sense of [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]. We call this pair the **cotangent phase space** of $Q$.

In an induced chart $(q^1,\ldots,q^n,p_1,\ldots,p_n)$, $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$ and $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$. A mathematical **observable** on this phase space means a smooth function $F:T^*Q\to\mathbb R$; this definition does not assert that a measurement has been performed or that every such function is physically measurable.

For an interpreted particle model, assign coordinates $q^i$ their declared units and assign the conjugate covector components $p_i$ units of action divided by the units of $q^i$. Thus $\theta$ and $\omega$ have action units, conventionally joule-seconds, and a bracket of quantities with units \([F]\) and \([G]\) has units \([F][G]/(\text{action})\). These are dimensional interpretations of the model, not additional mathematical premises. The use of $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ is exactly the use in the smooth cotangent-bundle suppliers; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Lorentz metric convention, an inertial affine chart, and the cotangent phase-space data specified above.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ only; no full axiom of choice is used.

[F1] [[thm-sr-proper-orthochronous-lorentz-algebra]]: $SO^+(1,3)$ is the determinant-one Lorentz subgroup preserving the selected future cone.

[L1] [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]]: the current H0 draft defines finite-dimensional $T^*Q$ with $\theta=p_i\,dq^i$, $\omega=-d\theta=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ only. Its H25 Step 1 record is ready and hash-current; that records readiness but is not independent proof approval. The carrier remains status draft with no pipeline_run binding; its definition and sign interface match here, and proof provenance is not-applicable.

[F2] [[def-symplectic-and-hamiltonian-lie-group-action]]: the Lie-algebra dual is the space of linear functionals $\mathfrak g^*=\mathcal L(\mathfrak g,\mathbb R)$; the library uses $\xi_M(z)=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp(-s\xi)\cdot z$ and $d\mu^\xi=-\iota_{\xi_M}\omega$.

[F3] [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]]: a nonempty regular level of a smooth map between finite-dimensional manifolds is an embedded submanifold of codimension the target dimension.

[F4] [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]: in an orthonormal inertial chart the timelike set has exactly two connected components $T_+$ and $T_-$; the chosen future cone is the component containing the positive time axis, and every invertible Lorentz map carries each component onto one component.

[F5] [[lem-lorentz-lie-algebra-structure]]: the derivatives at identity of $C^1$ curves in $O(1,3)$ satisfy $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, and this condition defines a six-dimensional linear subspace closed under the matrix commutator.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the selected time orientation, affine action, cotangent convention, and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 On $GL(4,\mathbb R)$ define $\Phi(L)=L^T\eta L$ with values in the ten-dimensional space of symmetric matrices. At $\Phi(L)=\eta$, its derivative is $D\Phi_L(\Delta)=\Delta^T\eta L+L^T\eta\Delta$. For any symmetric $S$, set $\Delta=L\eta^{-1}S/2$; using $L^T\eta L=\eta$ and $S^T=S$, each summand equals $S/2$. Thus $D\Phi_L$ is onto. [F3, algebra]

2.1 Every point of $\Phi^{-1}(\eta)$ is regular by step 1.1, and the level is nonempty because it contains $I$. Thus [F3] makes $O(1,3)=\Phi^{-1}(\eta)$ an embedded six-dimensional submanifold of $GL(4,\mathbb R)$. For $L\in O(1,3)$, $Le_0$ is timelike and $L$ is a homeomorphism of the timelike set; [F4] implies that $L$ preserves the selected future component exactly when $Le_0$ lies in that component. Since $e_0$ is the positive time-axis vector, this is exactly $L^0{}_0>0$. Also $|L^0{}_0|\ge1$, and taking determinants in $L^T\eta L=\eta$ gives $(\det L)^2=1$. Therefore $\det L=1$ and $L^0{}_0>0$ select an open subset of $O(1,3)$. By [F1] this subset is $SO^+(1,3)$. Matrix multiplication and inversion restrict smoothly from $GL(4)$, so this subgroup is a six-dimensional Lie group. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Give $G=\mathbb R^4\times SO^+(1,3)$ the product manifold structure from step 2.1 and multiplication $(a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L)$. Both parenthesizations of a triple product equal $(a+\Lambda b+\Lambda Lc,\Lambda LM)$; the identity is $(0,I)$; and direct substitution shows $(-\Lambda^{-1}a,\Lambda^{-1})$ is a left and right inverse. Multiplication and inversion are smooth because matrix multiplication and inversion on $SO^+(1,3)$ are smooth and the translation operations are smooth. The affine matrix map $\rho(a,\Lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is injective, has smooth inverse onto its image by block projection, and is a group homomorphism because matrix multiplication gives $\rho(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L)$. The product manifold tangent at identity is $\mathbb R^4\times T_I SO^+(1,3)$. By [F5], the latter tangent space is contained in the six-dimensional space of matrices satisfying $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$; both have dimension six by step 2.1 and [F5], so they are equal. Hence $d\rho_I(a,A)=\begin{pmatrix}A&a\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. A group homomorphism carries left-invariant vector fields to related left-invariant fields: differentiating $\rho\circ L_g=L_{\rho(g)}\circ\rho$ gives this relation. Related fields' brackets are related, since applying each bracket to a smooth test function and expanding $X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$ gives the same identity after composition with $\rho$. For matrices $M,N$, the left-invariant fields on $GL(5)$ are $g\mapsto gM$ and $g\mapsto gN$; differentiating these fields gives their commutator at the identity as $MN-NM$. Thus the bracket of two pair matrices is $\begin{pmatrix}[A,B]&Ab-Ba\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, yielding $[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B])$. [F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The cotangent lift preserves the covector-tangent pairing: $p'(dx')=(\Lambda^{-T}p)(\Lambda dx)=p(dx)$. For the one-parameter element $\exp(-s(a,A))$, differentiation of $x'=\Lambda_s x+a_s$ gives the fundamental field $(-(a+Ax),A^Tp)$ on $(x,p)$; its negative is the positive cotangent-lifted field $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pairing the covector with the positive base generator gives $\ell=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c)$. [L1, F2, A1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Antisymmetry of $A^{bc}$ gives $J_{bc}A^{bc}=-2p_bA^b{}_cx^c$: expand $J_{bc}=x_bp_c-x_cp_b$ and interchange $b,c$ in the first term. Substitution yields $\ell=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$. The definitions of $P,J$ then give $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$ from $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[p]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, and $[c]=\mathrm{m/s}$. [L1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $Q$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold as in [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]], and write its cotangent phase space in induced coordinates $(q^i,p_i)$. With $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$, define $X_H$ by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and define the Poisson bracket by $\{F,G\}:=X_G(F)$. Then

$$X_H=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i},\qquad \{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}.$$

The bracket is coordinate independent and makes smooth functions a Poisson algebra. If $H_t$ is smooth on an open time-dependent domain $D\subset\mathbb R\times T^*Q$, each solution of $\dot z=X_{H_t}(z)$ has local uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial data and parameters; on its actual interval,

$$\frac{d}{dt}F(t,z(t))=\partial_tF+\{F,H_t\}.$$

No completeness or global flow is asserted. If $H$ is smooth, each local time-$t$ flow map preserves ω.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $Q$, its canonical symplectic cotangent phase space, a smooth $H$, and where used a smooth time-dependent Hamiltonian $H_t$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume countable choice ACω, meaning every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]]: in induced coordinates $\omega=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$; observables are smooth real functions.

[F2] [[thm-smooth-functions-form-a-poisson-algebra]]: the symplectic bracket is coordinate independent, skew, bilinear, satisfies Leibniz and Jacobi.

[F3] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: a $C^1$ locally Lipschitz vector field has unique local solutions, and a smooth vector field depending smoothly on initial data and parameters has smooth local solution dependence.

## Proof

1.1 Write $X_H=A^i\partial_{q^i}+B_i\partial_{p_i}$. Contraction gives $\iota_{X_H}\omega=A^i dp_i-B_i dq^i$. Equating with $dH=H_{q^i}dq^i+H_{p_i}dp_i$ yields $A^i=H_{p_i}$, $B_i=-H_{q^i}$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 Substitution into $X_G(F)$ gives the displayed coordinate bracket. Its intrinsic definition from ω makes the formula invariant under cotangent coordinate changes; [F2] supplies the Poisson identities. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Along a solution, the chain rule gives $dF/dt=F_t+dF(X_{H_t})$; the definition of the bracket and skewness give $dF(X_{H_t})=X_{H_t}(F)=\{F,H_t\}$. [given, F2, step 1.1, calculus]

2.2 Smoothness of $H_t$ makes its coordinate Hamiltonian vector field smooth. Applying [F3] on the open domain yields unique local solutions and smooth dependence wherever solutions remain in that domain. This conclusion says nothing about extension beyond that interval. [given, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For smooth autonomous $H$, $d\omega=0$ and $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ imply $\mathcal L_{X_H}\omega=d\iota_{X_H}\omega+\iota_{X_H}d\omega=d^2H=0$; differentiating the pullback along the local flow therefore gives zero, and its initial value is ω, so the flow preserves ω. [given, F1, step 1.1, calculus] ∎

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_{\omega}$ and let $(M^{2n},\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold. A finite family of smooth functions $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ defined on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ is a **regular primary constraint family** on

$$C:=\{z\in U:\chi_1(z)=\cdots=\chi_r(z)=0\}$$

when $d\chi_1(z),\ldots,d\chi_r(z)$ are linearly independent at every $z\in C$. The regular-level theorem [[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] then gives $C$ its embedded-submanifold structure and $T_zC=\bigcap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$. For functions $F,G$ on $U$, write $F\approx G$ when $F|_C=G|_C$; thus $F\approx0$ means that $F$ vanishes on $C$, without requiring it to vanish off $C$.

Given a smooth canonical Hamiltonian $H_c$ on $U$ and multiplier functions $u^a(t)$, the **total generator** is

$$H_T(t,z):=H_c(t,z)+\sum_{a=1}^r u^a(t)\chi_a(z).$$

The functions $u^a$ are independent parameter functions; the definition does not assert that their equations determine them. If $H_c$ is an energy and $\chi_a$ has units \([\chi_a]\), then $u^a$ has units energy divided by \([\chi_a]\), so every term in $H_T$ has the same units. A later constraint, if generated by consistency, is not declared primary by this definition.

## Statement

Let $(P^{2n},\omega)$ be symplectic, and let $N=\{\chi_1=\cdots=\chi_r=0\}$ be a regular embedded level surface with $\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}=0$ on $N$. Then $\ker(\omega|_N)$ is exactly the rank-$r$ distribution spanned by the restricted Hamiltonian vector fields $X_{\chi_a}$. This distribution is involutive. Around every point of $N$, its leaves admit smooth Frobenius coordinates $(s^1,\ldots,s^r,y^1,\ldots,y^{2n-2r})$, and the local leaf space has a unique smooth closed nondegenerate two-form $\omega_{\mathrm{red}}$ whose pullback is $\omega|_N$. Thus regular first-class constraints yield a local symplectic quotient. No global orbit-space regularity follows from these hypotheses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold, a regular common level $N$, and constraints whose mutual brackets vanish on $N$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: assume countable choice ACω, the exact choice strength used by the cotangent smooth-structure supplier; no full axiom of choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]: $T_zN=\cap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$.

[F2] [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]: $\omega$ is closed and nondegenerate; $\iota_{X_f}\omega=df$.

[F3] [[def-symplectic-orthogonal-complement]]: $W^\omega=\{v:\omega(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\in W\}$, equivalently the inverse image of the annihilator under $\omega^\flat$.

[F4] [[prop-symplectic-double-orthogonal-and-dimension-identities]]: for each tangent subspace $W$, $\dim W+\dim W^\omega=\dim P$.

[F5] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: smooth linear ODEs have unique local solutions smoothly dependent on parameters.

[F6] [[thm-frobenius-local-coordinate-theorem]]: a smooth involutive rank-$r$ distribution has local coordinates in which leaves are the $s$-coordinate slices with $y$ constant.

[F7] [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]: the convention is $\{F,G\}=X_G(F)$ and $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$.


## Proof

1.1 For $w\in T_zN$, [F1] gives $d\chi_a(w)=0$, hence $\omega(X_{\chi_a},w)=0$ and each $X_{\chi_a}\in(T_zN)^\omega$. The $d\chi_a$ are independent, so their images under the isomorphism $\omega^\flat$ are independent; therefore these $r$ vectors are independent. The level has codimension $r$, and [F4] gives $\dim(T_zN)^\omega=r$, so they span the symplectic orthogonal. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, linear algebra]

1.2 On $N$, $d\chi_b(X_{\chi_a})=\{\chi_b,\chi_a\}=0$ by first-classness and [F7], so each $X_{\chi_a}$ is tangent. Their independence from step 1.1 implies $r\le\dim N=2n-r$, hence $r\le n$. The radical of the restricted form is $T_zN\cap(T_zN)^\omega$; since the orthogonal is already spanned by tangent $X_{\chi_a}$, this intersection is exactly that span. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, linear algebra]

2.1 For smooth kernel fields $U,V$ and any tangent field $W$, apply $d\omega_N=0$ to $(U,V,W)$. All terms containing contractions with $U$ or $V$ vanish, leaving $\omega_N([U,V],W)=0$. Thus ([U,V]) is again in the kernel and the distribution is involutive. [given, F2, step 1.2, exterior-calculus identity]

2.2 The Frobenius frame proof solves a transverse linear matrix ODE to straighten a local frame. Its coefficients are smooth, so [F5] gives a smooth local solution in transverse coordinates; the initial matrix is identity, so its determinant remains nonzero after shrinking the coordinate neighborhood. The resulting frame is involutive and [F6] supplies local $(s,y)$ coordinates. This explicitly supplies the parameter dependence needed in that construction. [given, F5, F6, step 2.1]

3.1 Since every $\omega_N$-kernel vector is tangent to the $s$-leaves, the contraction of $\omega_N$ with $\partial_{s^a}$ vanishes. Therefore its coordinate expression has no $ds^a$ factor. [step 1.2, step 2.2, linear algebra]

3.2 For each leaf vector $U$, Cartan's identity gives $\mathcal L_U\omega_N=d\iota_U\omega_N+\iota_Ud\omega_N=0$. Thus the coefficients of the remaining $dy^i\wedge dy^j$ form are independent of $s$; they define a form $\omega_{\mathrm{red}}$ on the local $y$-space and the coordinate projection pulls it back to $\omega_N$. It is closed because $d\omega_N=0$, and nondegenerate because its kernel would lift to a vector in $TN$ orthogonal to all of $TN$, hence to the already-quotiented kernel. [given, F2, step 2.2, step 3.1, exterior-calculus identity] ∎

## Statement

In affine Minkowski space with inertial coordinates $x^0,x^i$ measured in metres and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, let $m\ge0$ and let

$$\Sigma_m^+=\{(x,p): -p_0=P^0=\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2},\ p_0<0\},$$

where $\mathbf p\ne0$ when $m=0$, and write $P^i=p_i$ for the spatial raised momentum components. The characteristic flow of the restricted canonical form is $(x,p)\mapsto(x+\alpha P,p)$, and its orbit space is globally diffeomorphic to $B_m=\mathbb R^3_a\times\mathbb R^3_p$ for $m>0$, or $\mathbb R^3_a\times(\mathbb R^3_p\setminus\{0\})$ for $m=0$, by

$$a^i=x^i-\frac{P^i}{P^0}x^0,\qquad p_i=p_i.$$

The reduced symplectic form is $da^i\wedge dp_i$. The quotient is Hausdorff and second countable and each full characteristic line meets each slice $x^0=ct$ exactly once. This is an explicit free flat quotient, not a conclusion about arbitrary first-class systems.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model, its canonical cotangent form, and the specified future shell with $P^0>0$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume countable choice ACω, meaning every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]]: $\omega=\sum_a dx^a\wedge dp_a$ and $\theta=p_a\,dx^a$.

[F2] [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: inertial affine coordinates have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, with fixed $c>0$.

[F3] [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]: a Hamiltonian depending only on momentum has characteristic field $(\partial H/\partial p_a)\partial_{x^a}$.

[F4] [[thm-rpm-h-first-class-local-reduction]]: the characteristic kernel is the null direction of the restricted form; the present statement supplies explicit additional global coordinates.

## Proof

1.1 Solving the shell equation gives $p_0=-P^0$ with $P^0=\sqrt{m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2}>0$; for $m=0$ the exclusion $\mathbf p=0$ makes $P^0>0$. Thus $y=x^0/P^0$ and $a^i=x^i-(P^i/P^0)x^0$ are smooth shell coordinates, with inverse $x^0=yP^0, x^i=a^i+yP^i$. These formulas prove a diffeomorphism $\Sigma_m^+\cong\mathbb R_y\times B_m$. [given, A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Since the constraint depends only on $p$, [F3] gives its characteristic field $X_C=P^a\partial_{x^a}$; [F4] identifies this direction with the characteristic leaves used for reduction. The flow sends $y\mapsto y+\alpha$ while fixing $a,p$. Hence two points are in the same full orbit exactly when their $a,p$ labels agree, and the quotient map is the product projection to $B_m$. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, Hamilton equations]

2.1 The spaces $\mathbb R^3$ and $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ are Hausdorff second-countable manifolds; their product with $\mathbb R^3_a$ has the same properties. Product projection is a smooth submersion with global section $y=0$, establishing the asserted global quotient directly. [step 1.1, step 1.2, Euclidean topology]

2.2 In shell coordinates $x^0=yP^0, x^i=a^i+yP^i$, so $dx^0=P^0\,dy+y\,dP^0$ and $dx^i=da^i+P^i\,dy+y\,dP^i$. Since $p_0=-P^0$, expanding the canonical form gives

$$\omega=da^i\wedge dp_i+dy\wedge(P^i dp_i-P^0dP^0)+y\,dP^i\wedge dp_i.$$

Differentiating $(P^0)^2=m^2c^2+|\mathbf p|^2$ gives $P^0dP^0=P^i dp_i$, so the (dy)-term vanishes. The matrix $\partial P^i/\partial p_j=\delta^{ij}$ is symmetric, so $dP^i\wedge dp_i=0$. The restricted form is therefore the pullback of $da^i\wedge dp_i$, which is nondegenerate on $B_m$. [given, F1, step 1.1, differential calculus]

3.1 Along every orbit $x^0(\alpha)=x^0(0)+\alpha P^0$, with $P^0>0$, so each level $x^0=ct$ is attained at the unique parameter $\alpha=(ct-x^0(0))/P^0$. [step 1.2, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Use the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ throughout. In the flat case, **Minkowski spacetime** means the affine model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: $A$ is an affine space, $\eta$ is a nondegenerate Lorentz form on its four-dimensional displacement space, and $C^+$ selects the future cone. In the curved case, a **background spacetime** means a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the metric and time orientation are fixed data, not dynamical unknowns here. No field equation or completeness assumption is included.

A **massive worldline** on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a $C^2$ curve $x:I\to M$ with future-directed timelike tangent $T=dx/ds$ at every parameter value. This is the smooth subclass of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. A **null worldline** is a $C^2$ curve with nonzero future-directed null tangent everywhere. Its tangent has no proper-time normalization: $g(T,T)=0$, so the massive proper-time formula does not apply. In the flat model these are affine curves into $A$ with tangent in the selected future timelike or null cone from [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]].

## Definition

Let $\mathcal D$ be an open subset of the time-dependent tangent bundle $\mathbb R\times TQ$ of a finite-dimensional smooth manifold $Q$, and let $L:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For fixed $t$, the **fibre derivative** is the map

$$\mathbb F L(t,q,v)=(t,q,p),\qquad p(w)=\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{s=0}L(t,q,v+sw),$$

as in [[def-fibre-derivative-and-legendre-transform-of-a-lagrangian]]. In induced coordinates $p_i=\partial L/\partial v^i$.

The Lagrangian is **regular** at $(t,q,v)$ when the velocity Hessian $(\partial^2L/\partial v^i\partial v^j)$ is invertible there; regularity gives only a local inverse branch. It is **hyperregular on a declared domain** when $\mathbb F L$ is a diffeomorphism from that entire domain onto an open subset of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$.

It is **almost regular on a declared domain $\mathcal D_0\subseteq\mathcal D$** when the following are all assumed: $\mathbb F L|_{\mathcal D_0}$ has constant rank; its image $N$ is an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R\times T^*Q$; its corestriction $\mathcal D_0\to N$ is a surjective submersion (its differential is surjective at every point); and every fibre of that corestriction is connected. These hypotheses are not consequences of singularity alone.

## Statement

Let $L(q,v)$ be $C^2$ on a conic open subset of a tangent bundle, and suppose $L(q,av)=aL(q,v)$ for every $a>0$ in its domain. At each nonzero $v$,

$$v^iL_{v^i}=L,\qquad L_{v^iv^j}v^i=0,\qquad E_L:=v^iL_{v^i}-L=0.$$

Consequently the velocity Hessian is singular and the fibre derivative cannot be a local diffeomorphism there; a regular Legendre equivalence theorem cannot be applied. These conclusions do not imply that the motion is static or that the Lagrangian has a specified constraint surface.

## Definition

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

## Definition

For this nonrelativistic framework, a Newtonian event-coordinate domain is the Cartesian product $I\times\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cartesian-product]]), where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open time interval as in [[def-interval]], measured in seconds, and $\mathbb R^3$ has the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] (the norm properties follow from [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]); lengths are measured in metres as in [[def-td-si-quantities]]. A Galilean inertial chart labels events in such a domain by coordinates $(t,\mathbf x)$. If a second chart uses the translated time domain $I'=I+\tau$, the allowed coordinate changes are
$$t'=t+\tau,\qquad \mathbf x'=R\mathbf x+\mathbf a-\mathbf b t,$$
where $\tau$ is a constant time shift measured in seconds, $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation measured in metres, $\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant boost velocity measured in metres per second, and $R\in M_{3\times3}(\mathbb R)$ is a dimensionless constant matrix ([[def-matrix-space]]) satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ using matrix transpose and product ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), with $I_3$ the identity matrix. In the coordinate formula, $(R\mathbf x)_i:=\sum_{k<3}R_{ik}x_k$ for $i<3$. Thus time is absolute in this model and no Lorentzian structure is used. Here “frame” means this coordinate chart, not an observer congruence or a basis/tetrad field.

For a finite point-mass representation with $N\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $N\ge1$, masses $m_i>0$ in kg at positions $\mathbf x_i\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres for $i<N$, assume $M:=\sum_{i<N}m_i>0$ ([[def-finite-sum]]) and define the center-of-mass coordinates by $X_{\mathrm{cm},j}:=M^{-1}\sum_{i<N}m_i x_{i,j}$ for $j<3$; these three real coordinates form $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}$. The masses are invariant under the allowed chart changes. Other mechanical models must supply their total mass and center-of-mass map; this thermodynamic item does not construct those quantities for a continuum or field model. Every admitted mechanical model must also supply center-of-mass maps and velocities that transform under the displayed Galilean chart changes by $\mathbf X'_{\mathrm{cm}}(t')=R\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}(t)+\mathbf a-\mathbf b t$ and $\mathbf v'_{\mathrm{cm}}=R\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}-\mathbf b$, where $t'=t+\tau$; these are kinematic compatibility conditions, not dynamical theorems about arbitrary mechanical models. When the model supplies a center-of-mass position $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-function-space]]), its velocity at a time $t$ is the componentwise limit $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}(t)=\lim_{h\to0}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}(t+h)-\mathbf X_{\mathrm{cm}}(t))/h$ through $H_t:=\{h\in\mathbb R:t+h\in I,\ h\ne0\}$ ([[def-function-limit]]), when that limit exists. A center-of-mass rest frame is a Galilean inertial chart in which this velocity is zero; the adopted covariance condition allows the pure boost $\mathbf b=\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ to select one whenever the velocity is defined. For a fixed closed body with total mass $M>0$ in kg, its separately tracked translational kinetic energy in a selected inertial chart is $K_{\mathrm{cm}}=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\|_2^2$ in joules; under a pure boost it is $K'_{\mathrm{cm}}=\tfrac12M\|\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}-\mathbf b\|_2^2$.

In this framework $U$ denotes the scalar internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame. Bulk translational kinetic energy and any separately tracked external-field potential energy are excluded from $U$. The model treats $U$ as invariant between rest charts that differ only by spatial translation or orthogonal orientation, and fixes its numerical zero, including any retained or subtracted constituent rest-energy offsets, consistently across the composition changes it admits. This is a nonrelativistic modeling convention, not a derived energy-transformation law.

## Definition

A thermodynamic system $s$ is a model-selected body or collection of bodies together with a specified outer boundary $\partial s$. The boundary separates the system from its environment for the purpose of classifying transfers; it need not be a material wall. A compound system has named subsystems inside one outer boundary. Transfers between its subsystems are internal to the compound; only transfers across $\partial s$ are external.

The model specifies which transfers across $\partial s$ are permitted. A system is closed when no matter crosses its outer boundary; energy may cross. A system is open when only the named matter species and other named transfer channels may cross its boundary. A system or compound is isolated when no matter or energy crosses its outer boundary. These terms classify the declared model boundary, not the accuracy with which a real apparatus approximates it.

This boundary classification alone asserts neither an energy-balance law nor equilibration.

## Statement

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

**Given:** The open domain, $C^1$ map, zero, dimensions, and invertible derivative minor in the Statement.

[F2] [[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]]: a square linear map is invertible when it has a two-sided linear inverse.

[L1] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]]: for $G:\mathbb R^{m+q}\supset W\to\mathbb R^q$ with $m,q\ge1$, $G(a,b)=0$, and invertible derivative in the second block, the local zero set is a unique $C^1$ graph, with derivative $D\varphi=-(D_yG)^{-1}D_xG$.

[L2] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: a $C^1$ map between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ with invertible derivative at a point is a local $C^1$ bijection with a $C^1$ inverse.

[L3] [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]: linear maps between Euclidean spaces have coordinate matrices and are bounded, hence continuous; a coordinate permutation is an invertible linear map.

## Statement

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Suppose that for every $x\in C$ there is a nondegenerate interval $J_x\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $1$ such that $\lambda x\in C$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda\in J_x$. Here nondegenerate means that $J_x$ contains a point different from $1$; $1$ may be an endpoint. Then

$$f(x)=Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\,\partial_j f(x)\qquad(x\in C).$$

The radial identity need only hold on one side of $1$: openness of $C$ and $C^1$ regularity supply an ambient derivative, and the interval makes $1$ a nonisolated point at which that derivative is determined by the radial identity. This uses the same function on the same domain; it asserts nothing about a family of functions on different tagged domains.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open domain $C$, the $C^1$ function $f$, and for each $x\in C$ the stated radial homogeneity on a nondegenerate interval containing $\lambda=1$.

[F1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: If $f$ and $g$ are totally differentiable at the relevant points, then $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $x\in C$. Openness of $C$ and continuity of $\lambda\mapsto\lambda x$ give an open interval $K_x\subset(0,\infty)$ around $1$ with $\lambda x\in C$ for $\lambda\in K_x$. Define $g:K_x\to\mathbb R$ by $g(\lambda)=f(\lambda x)$. By [F1], $g'(1)=Df(x)[x]$. This ambient derivative exists even if $1$ is an endpoint of the interval $J_x$ on which homogeneity is assumed. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Since $J_x$ is a nondegenerate interval containing $1$, it contains points $\lambda\ne1$ arbitrarily close to $1$, also lying in $K_x$. For these points, homogeneity and $g(1)=f(x)$ give $(g(\lambda)-g(1))/(\lambda-1)=f(x)$. The ambient derivative in step 1.1 exists, so its limit along this possibly one-sided set is $g'(1)=f(x)$. Therefore $f(x)=Df(x)[x]$, and writing the total derivative in Euclidean coordinates gives $Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\partial_j f(x)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Use the adopted $C^2$ entropy with $S_{c,U}>0$ on this chart.

For every $\lambda>0$, admit scaling of every $x\in C$, so $C\subseteq B_{c,\lambda}$, and retain the distinct scaled-system tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. The image $C^{(\lambda)}:=\delta_\lambda(C)$ is a chart in $D_{c^{(\lambda)}}$. Adopt a coordinate-preserving material-law transport $j_{c,\lambda}:C^{(\lambda)}\to C$ defined in numerical coordinates by $j_{c,\lambda}(y)=y$, and adopt entropy preservation under that transport:

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(y)=S_c(j_{c,\lambda}(y))\qquad(y\in C^{(\lambda)}).$$

The transport identifies the constitutive numerical law used for bodies in this branch; it does not equate their physical identities or material tags. ## Statement

Let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^m$ be open with $k,m\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose the map $(u,z)\mapsto(x,z):=(D_u f(u,z),z)$ restricts to a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open neighborhoods, with inverse $(x,z)\mapsto(g(x,z),z)$. Define

$$\widehat f(x,z):=f(g(x,z),z)-x\cdot g(x,z).$$

Then $\widehat f$ is $C^2$ and

$$d\widehat f=-g\cdot dx+D_z f(g(x,z),z)\cdot dz.$$

This is a local statement. Existence of the inverse chart is a hypothesis; the lemma asserts no global inverse or boundary transform.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open domain, a $C^2$ function $f$, and a $C^1$ inverse chart $g$ for $(u,z)\mapsto(D_u f(u,z),z)$.

[F1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: Differentiating a composition of totally differentiable maps gives the composed derivative.

[F2] [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism is a bijection between open neighborhoods whose map and inverse are both $C^1$.

[F3] [[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]]: Differentiation of a bounded-bilinear product obeys the sum of the two product terms.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The inverse identity gives $D_u f(g(x,z),z)=x$. By [F1], differentiating the composition in $\widehat f$ gives $d[f(g(x,z),z)]=x\cdot dg+D_z f(g(x,z),z)\cdot dz$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Apply [F3] componentwise to the finite scalar products in $x\cdot g$ to obtain $d[x\cdot g]=g\cdot dx+x\cdot dg$. Subtracting this from step 1.1 cancels the $x\cdot dg$ terms and yields the stated differential. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The coefficient functions $g$ and $D_zf(g,z)$ are $C^1$, since $g$ is $C^1$, $f$ is $C^2$, and [F1] applies to their compositions. The first partial derivatives of $\widehat f$ are therefore $C^1$, so $\widehat f$ is $C^2$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $P\ge1$ named phase branches of the same finite species list occupy a separated compound at an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint with the fixed totals and exact feasible set declared by [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. Assume each phase lies in an open C2 single-phase chart with finite positive temperature. For every pair of phases, assume the following about the feasible set at this endpoint: each named exchange channel permits a sufficiently small nonzero amount of transfer in both directions, while all other state coordinates may be held fixed.

Then, for every pair $\alpha,\beta$:
- if energy exchange is permitted, $T_\alpha=T_\beta$;
- if volume exchange is permitted, $p_\alpha/T_\alpha=p_\beta/T_\beta$, and if energy exchange is also permitted then $p_\alpha=p_\beta$;
- if species $j$ is transferable, $\mu_{\alpha,j}/T_\alpha=\mu_{\beta,j}/T_\beta$, and if energy exchange is also permitted then $\mu_{\alpha,j}=\mu_{\beta,j}$.

The pressure and chemical potentials are the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. The theorem makes no equality claim for a retained coordinate, a one-sided boundary exchange, or a channel absent from the declared feasible set. It is a model deduction, not evidence that these phases or exchange channels occur in nature.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite number of named phase branches, a positive-mole composition chart, an attained global entropy maximum on the exact feasible set, C2 entropy on each phase chart, finite positive temperatures, additive separated-system coordinates and entropy, and the bilateral local feasibility of each exchange direction used below. Use SI units.

[A1] [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]: A stable endpoint attains a global maximum of total entropy on its exact feasible endpoint set; local maxima alone are not called stable equilibrium.

[F1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] and [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]: Phase amounts and states lie in the declared branch charts and exact feasible set; only the listed totals and exchanges may vary.

[F2] [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: For the specified separated compound, energy, volume, aligned species amounts, and entropy add; on each selected single-phase chart the entropy is finite and C2 with $S_U>0$.

[F3] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: $S_U=1/T$, $S_V=p/T$, and $S_{n_j}=-\mu_j/T$, each partial holding the other physical coordinates fixed.

[L1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: The derivative of a differentiable composition is the composition of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 Fix any pair $\alpha,\beta$ and an allowed energy transfer. For any fixed nonzero increment $h$ joules, bilateral local feasibility supplies the curve $U_\alpha(t)=U_\alpha^*+th$, $U_\beta(t)=U_\beta^*-th$ for all sufficiently small $t$ of either sign, with all other coordinates fixed. The total entropy along this curve has a local maximum at $t=0$ by [A1]. Its derivative exists by [F2]; the right difference quotients are nonpositive and the left difference quotients are nonnegative, so the derivative is zero. By additivity and [L1], this derivative is $h(S_{\alpha,U}-S_{\beta,U})$. Since $h\ne0$, $S_{\alpha,U}=S_{\beta,U}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, L1, construct]

2.1 By [F3], $S_{\alpha,U}=1/T_\alpha$ and $S_{\beta,U}=1/T_\beta$. Both temperatures are finite and positive, so equality of the reciprocals gives $T_\alpha=T_\beta$. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If volume transfer is permitted, take a nonzero increment $k$ in $\mathrm{m^3}$ and vary $V_\alpha(t)=V_\alpha^*+tk$, $V_\beta(t)=V_\beta^*-tk$ with both signs feasible. The same local-maximum quotient argument gives $k(S_{\alpha,V}-S_{\beta,V})=0$, hence $S_{\alpha,V}=S_{\beta,V}$. By [F3], $p_\alpha/T_\alpha=p_\beta/T_\beta$. When energy transfer is also permitted, step 2.1 gives equal positive temperatures, so $p_\alpha=p_\beta$. These are derivative pressures; a mechanical piston interpretation requires its separately declared coupling. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, L1, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 If species $j$ is transferable, vary its mole amounts by $n_{\alpha,j}(t)=n_{\alpha,j}^*+tq$ and $n_{\beta,j}(t)=n_{\beta,j}^*-tq$ for a nonzero increment $q$ in moles. Both signs are feasible. The same quotient argument gives $q(S_{\alpha,n_j}-S_{\beta,n_j})=0$, hence equal entropy partials. By [F3], $\mu_{\alpha,j}/T_\alpha=\mu_{\beta,j}/T_\beta$. If energy transfer is also permitted, step 2.1 gives equal positive temperatures and therefore equal chemical potentials. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, L1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Every pair was arbitrary, so the asserted pairwise equalities hold for all named phases and only for the channels whose bilateral feasibility was assumed. If $P=1$, there are no pairs and the conditions are vacuous. No derivative equality follows for a retained or boundary coordinate because its required two-sided feasible curve is absent. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Definition

Fix a family $I$ of primitive material labels. A tagged type $c\in I$ retains its identity even if another type has the same coordinate domain. A positive scale $\lambda>0$ is dimensionless and is represented by the separately tagged bulk copy $c^{(\lambda)}$ and map $\delta_\lambda$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A finite separated compound is a finite tuple of tagged scaled systems, with permutation and reassociation identifications and an empty unit type. Its state is a tuple of constituent equilibrium states; its extensive coordinate tuple is the sum specified by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] whenever the pair is admitted there.

The formal composition vector of a compound records, for each primitive label $c$, the sum of its positive scale coefficients. Two compounds have the same composition exactly when these vectors agree. The distinct **formal mass** $m(A)$ is the sum of all scale coefficients in $A$, a dimensionless bookkeeping quantity; it is not physical mass in kilograms, mole amount, energy, or volume. Same-composition compounds have equal formal mass. For states $A,B$ of the same compound type, write $A\prec B$ when the declared adiabatic-accessibility relation of [[def-td-adiabatic-accessibility]] admits that endpoint comparison. This definition does not infer accessibility from coordinate addition.

An equal-composition comparison is a comparison between states of types with the same formal composition vector. The later reaction-network definition may separately admit transitions between distinct composition types, but the mathematical supplier still requires equal formal mass at both endpoints. A physical application must state how its channel preserves the chosen formal mass and separately record its dimensioned conservation balances. The empty unit has one state and formal mass zero. ## Definition

## Postulate

Adopt the following axioms for $\prec$ on every declared pair of finite compounds with equal formal mass in [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]]. Initially this covers equal-composition adiabatic accessibility. If a later channel model admits comparisons between distinct composition types, the same axioms apply to those comparisons and all their finite scaled products; no cross-type transition is admitted by this postulate alone. They are assumptions of the operational model, not consequences of the process definition or of energy additivity.

**A1 (reflexivity).** $A\prec A$ for every state $A$.

**A2 (transitivity).** If $A\prec B$ and $B\prec C$, then $A\prec C$.

**A3 (consistency).** If $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every finite spectator compound $C$ for which both endpoint compounds are admitted and the resulting formal masses agree.

**A4 (scaling).** If $A\prec B$, then $\lambda A\prec\lambda B$ for every $\lambda>0$, using the tagged scaling maps of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]].

**A5 (splitting).** For each state $x$, positive $s<t$, and tagged scaled copies of its material, the state $t x$ is accessible in both directions to the separated pair $(s x,(t-s)x)$. This states reversible splitting of an equilibrium preparation into scaled copies, not additivity of arbitrary state functions.

**A6 (stability).** Let $A,B$ have equal formal mass. Let $Z_0,Z_1$ be fixed positive spectator compounds of equal formal mass, and let $\epsilon_n>0$ decrease to zero. If $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\prec B$.

Equality of formal masses in A6 is required so each comparison is defined; equality of composition vectors is not required when a declared model includes cross-type transitions. A6 is a limiting closure assumption on the relation; it does not assert continuity of any physical process or the existence of a limiting apparatus.

**S2 (unique finite-slope support).** At $x=(u_x,v_x)$, $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane through $x$, and it can be written
$$
u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0
$$
with finite $P_i(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_i}$. The map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$ is locally Lipschitz: every point has a neighborhood on which one finite Lipschitz constant bounds $\|P_i(x)-P_i(y)\|/\|x-y\|$. **S3 (connected relative boundary).** The boundary $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$, taken in the topology relative to $\Gamma_i$, is arcwise connected.

These are explicit adopted conditions. The slope $P_i$ is a geometric support parameter here; no equation identifying it with measured pressure is asserted. In particular, S1–S3 and A7 do not assert comparison hypothesis for products.

## Definition

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

## Scope

The integral may equal $+\infty$ for a nonnegative function. For an integrable signed or complex function it is finite. The measure $\mu$ is the reference measure: changing it can change an integral and any entropy defined from a density relative to it.

## Definition

Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

## Scope

The definition concerns a mathematical probability mixture and an assigned scalar energy. It does not assert that physical phases can be prepared, exchanged, or brought to equilibrium.

## Statement

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compact generator space, continuous energy, and Borel-probability mixture convention.

[A1] $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ is nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ is continuous.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]: a mixture is a Borel probability on $K$; its barycenter and mean energy are coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals; $a_{\rm mix}$ is their constrained infimum.

[F2] [[def-borel-probability-law-on-a-polish-space]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]: Borel probability measures integrate bounded Borel real functions, and the integral is linear.

[F3] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, closed bounded sets are compact; compact sets are closed and every sequence in a compact set has a convergent subsequence in the set.

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum and maximum.

## Proof



**Given:** The data in [A1] and the mixture definitions in [F1].

1.1 Define $\Phi(y)=(y,a(y))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and $G=\Phi(K)$. The map $\Phi$ is continuous. The set $G$ is bounded because $\Phi[K]$ is bounded on compact $K$; it is closed because from any convergent sequence $\Phi(y_n)$, [F3] gives a subsequence $y_{n_j}\to y\in K$, and continuity gives $\Phi(y_{n_j})\to\Phi(y)$. Thus [F3] makes $G$ compact. [A1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Any finite convex combination of more than $d+2$ points of $G\subset\mathbb R^{d+1}$ has an affine dependence: there are coefficients $c_i$, not all zero, with $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i g_i=0$. Both signs occur. If its positive weights are $\theta_i$, replacing them by $\theta_i-tc_i$, where $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$, preserves their sum and combination, keeps them nonnegative, and makes at least one zero. Repeating gives at most $d+2$ points. Pad shorter combinations by zero weights and repeat any fixed point of nonempty $G$. It follows that $\operatorname{conv}G$ is the continuous image of the compact finite-dimensional parameter set $G^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$, where $\Delta_{d+2}=\{\theta_i\ge0:\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$. This set is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F3]; the same sequential argument as in 1.1 shows its image is compact. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Its fiber $F_x=\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G\}$ is nonempty, since each finite convex combination of generators gives such a point, and compact, since it is a closed section of compact $\operatorname{conv}G$. Therefore [F4] gives a minimum $r_x$. A convex-combination representation of $(x,r_x)$ by points $(y_i,a(y_i))$ defines a finite atomic Borel probability $P_x$ with barycenter $x$ and energy $r_x$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Conversely, for any Borel probability $P$ on $K$, the vector-valued map $\Phi$ is bounded and coordinatewise integrable by [F2]. Its integral is in $\operatorname{conv}G$: for each $\epsilon>0$, uniform continuity of $\Phi$ gives a finite Borel partition of $K$ whose pieces have image diameter at most $\epsilon$. Choose a point in each nonempty piece and weight it by that piece's $P$-mass. The resulting finite convex combination differs coordinatewise from $\int\Phi\,dP$ by at most $\epsilon$; as $\operatorname{conv}G$ is closed by step 2.1, the integral belongs to it. If $\bar y(P)=x$, then $(x,\bar a(P))\in\operatorname{conv}G$, so $\bar a(P)\ge r_x$. Together with step 3.1 this proves that the all-measure infimum equals $r_x$ and is attained by $P_x$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.2 To prove lower semicontinuity, let $x_n\to x$ in $\operatorname{conv}K$ and pass to a subsequence along which $a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$ tends to its liminf. The values lie between $\min_K a$ and $\max_K a$, attained by [F4], so a further subsequence of $(x_n,a_{\rm mix}(x_n))$ converges. Each pair lies in the compact set $\operatorname{conv}G$ by step 4.1; its limit is therefore $(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G$. The minimum in the fiber at $x$ satisfies $a_{\rm mix}(x)\le r=\liminf_n a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

5.1 Combine minimizers $P_x$ and $P_z$ with weights $s$ and $1-s$, $0\le s\le1$. The combined finite measure has barycenter $sx+(1-s)z$ and energy $s a_{\rm mix}(x)+(1-s)a_{\rm mix}(z)$. By step 4.1, the minimum at the combined barycenter is no greater than this value. Hence $a_{\rm mix}$ is convex. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

5.2 The support reduction in 2.1 first gives at most $d+2$ atoms. If an optimal representation has more than $d+1$ positive weights, the points $y_i\in\mathbb R^d$ have an affine dependence $\sum_i c_i y_i=0$, $\sum_i c_i=0$. For sufficiently small positive $t$, both weight lists $\theta_i\pm t c_i$ remain nonnegative and preserve the barycenter. If $\sum_i c_i a(y_i)\ne0$, one of these lists strictly lowers energy, contradicting optimality; hence this sum is zero. Increase $t$ in one sign to the first value at which a positive coefficient becomes zero. The new weights preserve barycenter and energy and still attain the minimum; iteration leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights. [A1, F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Finally, let $g$ be any convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ with $g(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$. For the finite optimal measure from 4.1, finite Jensen (obtained by iterating the two-point convexity inequality) gives $g(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i g(y_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i a(y_i)=a_{\rm mix}(x)$. Since $a_{\rm mix}(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$ by the point mass at $y$, it is itself such a convex minorant and dominates every other one. [F1, step 5.1, step 5.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless phase-generator coordinates. A generator point $x\in K$ encodes one model-specified homogeneous phase state, with declared entropy per mole $s(x)$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$; let $s:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ as the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$, and let $\delta_x$ denote unit point mass at $x$. The vector integral $\int_Kx\,dP$ is taken coordinatewise. Assume every Borel probability mixture $P$ on $K$ with $\int_Kx\,dP(x)=\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks(x)\,dP(x)$. Then the entropy maximum over all such mixtures is attained by a finite atomic mixture with at most $d+1$ phase-generator states.

Here the integral uses the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map includes its physical entropy units and is part of the model; this theorem does not derive the microscopic meaning of entropy or assert that a physical phase domain is compact.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite integer $d\ge1$, the nonempty compact generator set $K$, continuous entropy map $s$, prescribed $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, coordinatewise barycenter convention, and feasibility of all Borel probability mixtures with that barycenter. The normalization is per mole, and no limit in system size is taken.

[A1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]]: A phase-generator point records a declared homogeneous branch state; coexistence mixtures must use the model's exact feasible totals.

[A2] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: Entropy is a finite state function on the declared physical states. Continuity of the restricted map $s$ on this particular compact $K$ is an explicit hypothesis of this theorem.

[F1] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and [[def-probability-measure]]: The Borel sigma algebra is generated by open subsets of $K$, and a probability measure on it is countably additive with total mass one.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: A nonnegative measurable function is integrated by the supremum of its simple-function integrals; an integrable real function has finite real integral.

[L2] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-compact-continuous-mixture-attainment]]: For nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$ and continuous $a:K\to\mathbb R$, every fixed barycenter $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ has an attained minimum of $\int_Ka\,dP$ over all Borel probability measures with that barycenter; a minimizer can be chosen atomic on at most $d+1$ points. Its current batch-12 carrier has this exact statement and is registered as a draft. Its proof has unresolved completion defects recorded in batch-13 cross-batch evidence: step 5.1 cites nonexistent step 2.2, and step 4.1 uses uniform continuity and a finite Borel partition without a supporting proof or cited supplier.

## Proof

1.1 By [A1], each generator is a declared model state and feasible mixtures obey the model's exact totals. By [L2], $|s(x)|\le M$ on $K$ for some finite $M$. Every open subset of $\mathbb R$ has open preimage under the continuous map $s$, and preimages preserve complements and countable unions, so preimages of Borel sets are Borel; hence $s$ is Borel measurable. For any feasible probability measure $P$ and any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le |s|$, write $\varphi=\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ on disjoint Borel sets; then
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP=\sum_jc_jP(A_j)\le M\sum_jP(A_j)\le M P(K)=M.
$$
By the integral definition [F2], $\int_K|s|\,dP\le M$, so $s$ is integrable. Set $a=-s$; it is continuous and integrable, and the signed-integral definition gives $\int_Ka\,dP=-\int_Ks\,dP$. The barycenter constraint is unchanged, so minimizing $\int_Ka\,dP$ over the same feasible set is equivalent to maximizing $\int_Ks\,dP$. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, L2, algebra]

1.2 By definition of $\operatorname{conv}K$, there are finitely many $x_i\in K$ and nonnegative weights $\theta_i$ with $\sum_i\theta_i=1$ and $\bar x=\sum_i\theta_ix_i$. Then $P_0:=\sum_i\theta_i\delta_{x_i}$ is a Borel probability measure with coordinatewise barycenter $\bar x$, so the fixed-barycenter feasible set is nonempty under the model assumption. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply the exact current statement of [L1] to $K$, $a$, and $\bar x$. Conditional on the batch-12 proof defects being resolved and its accepted proof supporting that statement, it supplies a minimizing Borel probability measure $P_*$ supported on at most $d+1$ points. By step 1.1, this same $P_*$ maximizes the physical entropy functional. No finite phase menu was assumed. [given, L1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Counterexample

Let the one-dimensional phase-generator domain be $K=(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$, which is noncompact, and let its dimensionless coordinate be $x$. Assign entropy per mole
$$
s(x)=s_0-a|x|,\qquad a>0,
$$
where $s_0>a>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. Consider all Borel probability mixtures on $K$ with fixed barycenter $\bar x=0$ and declare them feasible with entropy $\int_Ks\,dP$. This is a constructed mixture model, not a claim that a particular material has this phase domain.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The noncompact Borel domain $K$, the bounded positive continuous concave entropy function $s$, and the feasible probability mixtures with mean zero.

[F1] [[pthm-td-compact-continuous-phase-mixture]]: Its attainment claim requires a compact phase-generator domain; it makes no attainment assertion for this noncompact $K$.

[F2] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-probability-measure]], and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: Mixtures are countably additive Borel probability measures of total mass one, and their integrals use the stated measure convention.

## Verification

1.1 Since $0< s_0-a\le s(x)\le s_0$, every feasible $s$ is nonnegative and bounded. For $n\ge2$, put $A_n:=\{x\in K:|x|\ge1/n\}$. Their union is $K$; since $P(K)=1$, countable additivity implies $P(A_n)>0$ for some $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F2] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le (s_0-a/n)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F2] gives the inequality. The common strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is supported on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int s\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. This lies outside the compactness hypothesis in [F1] and exhibits a finite supremum without a maximizing mixture. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

The tagged bulk-scaling relation of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] together with the additive coordinate composition of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] forces the fixed-tag identity $S_c(\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x)$ for each material constitution $c$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A dimensionless positive tag $\tau$, positive state coordinates $U,V,n$, and the following formal family; $U,V,n$ use joules, cubic metres, and moles.

[A1] [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]: Independent separated systems may have a composition map that adds the admitted extensive coordinates, and the bulk scaling map may send a state of tag $c$ to a distinct tag $c^{(\lambda)}$.

[A2] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: Entropy is finite and concave on its specified convex domains, additive for admitted independent separated systems, and satisfies the tagged relation $S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x)$. The tag $c^{(\lambda)}$ is not silently identified with $c$.

[F1] [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]: Equilibrium charts use positive physical coordinates $(U,V,n)$ on a domain whose admitted single-phase regions may be open subsets of the corresponding Euclidean coordinate space.

[F2] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: $U,V,n$ have units joules, cubic metres, and moles; entropy has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

## Counterexample

1.1 Let tags be $\tau>0$, compose them by $\tau_A\oplus\tau_B=\tau_A+\tau_B$, and scale by $\tau^{(\lambda)}=\lambda\tau$. 2.1 For two separated states, define the compound tag as $\tau_A+\tau_B$ and the composition map to add $U,V,n$. Then
$S_{\tau_A+\tau_B}(U_A+U_B,V_A+V_B,n_A+n_B)=S_{\tau_A}(U_A,V_A,n_A)+S_{\tau_B}(U_B,V_B,n_B)$,

2.2 Under scaling, $S_{\lambda\tau}(\lambda U,\lambda V,\lambda n)=a\lambda U+b\lambda V+q\lambda\tau=\lambda S_\tau(U,V,n)$, so the tagged scaling relation in [A2] holds for every $\lambda>0$. [A1, A2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the same fixed tag $\tau$, however, $S_\tau(2U,2V,2n)=2aU+2bV+q\tau$ whereas $2S_\tau(U,V,n)=2aU+2bV+2q\tau$. Since $q\tau>0$, these values differ. Thus tagged scaling plus the stated additivity does not imply fixed-tag homogeneity. [given, A1, A2, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
